claim: The COVID-19 pandemic has resulted in more genomes of SARS-CoV-2 having been sequenced than any other organism on earth.
source: The COVID-19 pandemic has resulted in a step change in the scale of sequencing data, with more genomes of SARS-CoV-2 having been sequenced than any other organism on earth.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the scale of SARS-CoV-2 sequencing, presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Phylogenetic trees reveal key insights into SARS-CoV-2 by capturing the evolutionary history of the virus and allowing identification of transmission events and emergence of new variants.
source: These sequences reveal key insights when represented as a phylogenetic tree, which captures the evolutionary history of the virus, and allows the identification of transmission events and the emergence of new variants.
evidence: This claim describes the utility of phylogenetic trees based on established scientific understanding of their applications.

claim: Existing web-based tools for exploring phylogenies do not scale to the size of datasets now available for SARS-CoV-2.
source: However, existing web-based tools for exploring phylogenies do not scale to the size of datasets now available for SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is an assertion about the limitations of existing tools, which is later supported by comparative performance data in the Results section.

claim: Taxonium uses WebGL to allow the exploration of trees with tens of millions of nodes in the browser for the first time.
source: We have developed Taxonium, a new tool that uses WebGL to allow the exploration of trees with tens of millions of nodes in the browser for the first time.
evidence: This is a direct claim about the capabilities of Taxonium, supported by the technical implementation described in the manuscript and performance data.

claim: Taxonium links each node to associated metadata and supports mutation-annotated trees.
source: Taxonium links each node to associated metadata and supports mutation-annotated trees, which are able to capture all known genetic variation in a dataset.
evidence: This describes features of Taxonium that are demonstrated in the figures and methods sections.

claim: Mutation-annotated trees are able to capture all known genetic variation in a dataset.
source: Taxonium links each node to associated metadata and supports mutation-annotated trees, which are able to capture all known genetic variation in a dataset.
evidence: This is a statement about the capability of mutation-annotated trees, based on their design and implementation.

claim: Taxonium can be run entirely locally in the browser, from a server-based backend, or as a desktop application.
source: It can either be run entirely locally in the browser, from a server-based backend, or as a desktop application.
evidence: This describes the deployment options for Taxonium, which are detailed in the Methods section.

claim: A public tree of more than five million SARS-CoV-2 sequences is available at cov2tree.org.
source: We describe insights that analysing a tree of five million sequences can provide into SARS-CoV-2 evolution, and provide a tool at cov2tree.org for exploring a public tree of more than five million SARS-CoV-2 sequences.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the availability of a resource, which can be verified by visiting the website.

claim: Taxonium source code is available at github.com/theosanderson/taxonium.
source: Taxonium can be applied to any tree, and is available at taxonium.org, with source code at github.com/theosanderson/taxonium.
evidence: This is a factual statement about code availability that can be verified.

claim: GISAID recently surpassed 11 million SARS-CoV-2 sequences.
source: Open protocols were quickly generated for amplicon sequencing (Tyson et al., 2020), and allowed researchers across the globe to produce ever-growing genomic datasets stored both in the INSDC databases (Cochrane et al., 2016), and in GISAID (Shu and McCauley, 2017), with the latter recently surpassing 11 million sequences.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the size of the GISAID database, presented as current knowledge.

claim: New tools were developed to assign SARS-CoV-2 samples into lineages proposed by the community.
source: Importantly, new tools were also developed to understand the functional diversity of these samples, by assigning them into lineages proposed by the community (Rambaut et al., 2020; O'Toole et al., 2021), and allowing interactive exploration of trends in these data over time (Hodcroft, 2021; Chen et al., 2021; Tsueng et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work describing these tools.

claim: A phylogenetic tree is the fundamental representation of a viral epidemic for genomic epidemiology.
source: The fundamental representation of a viral epidemic for genomic epidemiology is a phylogenetic tree, which approximates the transmission tree and can allow insights into the direction of migration of viral lineages (Wohl et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the role of phylogenetic trees in genomic epidemiology, supported by citation and established scientific knowledge.

claim: Phylogenetic trees approximate the transmission tree and can allow insights into the direction of migration of viral lineages.
source: The fundamental representation of a viral epidemic for genomic epidemiology is a phylogenetic tree, which approximates the transmission tree and can allow insights into the direction of migration of viral lineages (Wohl et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Trees annotated with mutations at internal nodes capture information about parallel and convergent evolution.
source: When trees are annotated with the mutations that have occurred at each internal node, they capture information about parallel and convergent evolution, which can identify recurrent mutations of concern.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of how mutation-annotated trees work.

claim: Mutation-annotated trees can identify recurrent mutations of concern.
source: When trees are annotated with the mutations that have occurred at each internal node, they capture information about parallel and convergent evolution, which can identify recurrent mutations of concern.
evidence: This describes a capability of mutation-annotated trees based on their design.

claim: The construction of phylogenetic trees and the visualisation of these trees have been major bottlenecks preventing full-scale analyses of SARS-CoV-2 datasets.
source: In particular, the construction of phylogenetic trees, and the visualisation of these trees, have been major bottlenecks preventing full-scale analyses.
evidence: This is an assertion about computational challenges, which is supported by the comparative analysis of tools later in the manuscript.

claim: Nextstrain provides one of the most widely-used and important tools for exploring SARS-CoV-2 genetic diversity.
source: This has been an important approach, and has allowed Nextstrain (Hadfield et al., 2018) to provide one of the most widely-used and important tools for exploring SARS-CoV-2 genetic diversity.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance and usage of Nextstrain, supported by citation and general knowledge in the field.

claim: The Nextstrain pipeline downsamples sequences in a rational way and uses iqtree to assemble them into a tree.
source: Briefly, the Nextstrain pipeline downsamples sequences in a rational way, and then uses iqtree (Minh et al., 2020) to assemble them into a tree, assigns chronology and ancestral states to this tree using TreeTime (Sagulenko et al., 2018), and displays the results in a user-friendly interactive interface using Auspice (Hadfield et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the Nextstrain pipeline, supported by citations to the relevant tools.

claim: Nextstrain analyses are typically limited to approximately 4000 sequences.
source: All three of these post-downsampling stages are bottlenecks which prevent the use of full datasets, and so Nextstrain analyses are typically limited to ~4000 sequences – sampled in a structured way to ensure they either provide an overview of the pandemic or hone in on particular sequences of interest.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the scale limitations of Nextstrain, based on knowledge of the tool's typical usage.

claim: UShER permits larger trees to be built than ever previously.
source: Recently the development of UShER (Turakhia et al., 2021) has permitted larger trees to be built than ever previously.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the UShER publication.

claim: UShER takes a starting tree and incrementally adds sequences by maximum parsimony.
source: UShER takes a starting tree, built with iqtree or a similar approach, and incrementally adds sequences by maximum parsimony.
evidence: This describes the methodology of UShER, based on cited literature.

claim: For densely sampled sequencing efforts, UShER's approach still yields tree topologies of very high quality.
source: For densely sampled sequencing efforts, as in the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, such an approach still yields tree topologies of very high quality (Thornlow et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a publication evaluating UShER's performance.

claim: Chronumental uses stochastic gradient descent to efficiently construct chronologies from very large trees.
source: To turn this distance tree into a time tree, by estimating a time associated with each node in the tree, we recently developed Chronumental (Sanderson, 2021) which uses stochastic gradient descent to efficiently construct chronologies from very large trees, which was not possible with previous approaches.
evidence: This describes the methodology of Chronumental, supported by citation.

claim: Constructing chronologies from very large trees was not possible with previous approaches before Chronumental.
source: To turn this distance tree into a time tree, by estimating a time associated with each node in the tree, we recently developed Chronumental (Sanderson, 2021) which uses stochastic gradient descent to efficiently construct chronologies from very large trees, which was not possible with previous approaches.
evidence: This is a claim about the limitations of previous methods, implied by the development of Chronumental.

claim: Taxonium scales to trees with millions of nodes.
source: Here, we describe Taxonium, a web-based tool for for analysing and exploring large trees. Taxonium scales to trees with millions of nodes, and allows for rapid panning and zooming using WebGL.
evidence: This claim is supported by performance data presented later in the manuscript.

claim: Taxonium allows for rapid panning and zooming using WebGL.
source: Taxonium scales to trees with millions of nodes, and allows for rapid panning and zooming using WebGL.
evidence: This describes a technical feature of Taxonium, demonstrated in the implementation.

claim: Taxonium can display UShER mutation-annotated trees which capture genotype information in mutations at internal branches.
source: In addition to reading Newick format trees, Taxonium can also display UShER mutation-annotated trees which capture genotype information in mutations at internal branches.
evidence: This describes a capability of Taxonium demonstrated in the figures and methods.

claim: Taxonium permits searching for nodes by metadata or genotype.
source: It permits searching for nodes by metadata or genotype, and a range of annotation options.
evidence: This describes features of Taxonium shown in the interface screenshots.

claim: Taxonium is available in a server-backed mode which loads in seconds to allow exploration of all publicly available SARS-CoV-2 sequences.
source: Taxonium is available in a server-backed mode, which in a matter of seconds loads to allow exploration of all publicly available SARS-CoV-2 sequences, and also a fully client-side mode suitable for exploring custom datasets, including those with sensitive data.
evidence: This claim is supported by performance measurements provided in the Results section.

claim: Taxonium has a fully client-side mode suitable for exploring custom datasets, including those with sensitive data.
source: Taxonium is available in a server-backed mode, which in a matter of seconds loads to allow exploration of all publicly available SARS-CoV-2 sequences, and also a fully client-side mode suitable for exploring custom datasets, including those with sensitive data.
evidence: This describes a deployment mode of Taxonium detailed in the Methods section.

claim: A major bottleneck for previous approaches was the use of web technologies involving SVG or Canvas to visualize trees.
source: One major bottleneck for previous approaches was the use of web technologies involving SVG or Canvas to visualize the tree, which have performance limitations.
evidence: This is an assertion about limitations of previous visualization technologies, based on technical understanding.

claim: SVG and Canvas web technologies have performance limitations for tree visualization.
source: One major bottleneck for previous approaches was the use of web technologies involving SVG or Canvas to visualize the tree, which have performance limitations.
evidence: This is based on established technical knowledge about these rendering technologies.

claim: Taxonium uses WebGL, a web standard that allows a computer's GPU to display web graphics, for efficient visualisation of the tree.
source: We instead use WebGL, a web standard that allows a computer's GPU to display web graphics, for efficient visualisation of the tree – we implement this using DeckGL (Uber, 2016).
evidence: This describes the technical implementation of Taxonium, with citation to the DeckGL library.

claim: Taxonium implements WebGL visualization using DeckGL.
source: We instead use WebGL, a web standard that allows a computer's GPU to display web graphics, for efficient visualisation of the tree – we implement this using DeckGL (Uber, 2016).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the implementation, supported by citation.

claim: Rendering every node in a large tree would be too slow and would involve hundreds of nodes overplotted on each pixel when zoomed out.
source: Even so, rendering every node in the tree would still be too slow, and would involve hundreds of nodes overplotted on each pixel when a tree was zoomed out.
evidence: This is a technical inference about rendering performance based on the scale of the trees.

claim: Taxonium renders a sparsified version of the tree, with sparsification dependent on zoom level such that only nodes that overlap other nodes are excluded.
source: We address this by rendering a sparsified version of the tree, with the sparsification dependent on the zoom level such that only nodes that overlap other nodes are excluded (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the sparsification algorithm implemented in Taxonium, detailed in the Methods section.

claim: The input to Taxonium is a tree (e.g. in Newick format) and, optionally, metadata.
source: The input to Taxonium is a tree (e.g. in Newick format) and, optionally, metadata.
evidence: This describes the input requirements for Taxonium.

claim: Metadata is associated with each node of the tree, and the tree can be coloured by any chosen metadata item.
source: Metadata is associated with each node of the tree, and the tree can be coloured by any chosen metadata item.
evidence: This describes a feature of Taxonium shown in the interface.

claim: Colours in Taxonium are by default selected using an algorithm that hashes the metadata's string value into a unique colour.
source: Colours are by default selected using an algorithm that hashes the metadata's string value into a unique colour, ensuring consistency over time without the need for comprehensive look-up tables.
evidence: This describes the color assignment algorithm used in Taxonium.

claim: The tree in Taxonium can be searched based on metadata, with identified nodes circled.
source: In addition, the tree can be searched based on the metadata, with identified nodes circled.
evidence: This describes a search feature shown in the interface screenshots.

claim: Taxonium supports complex hierarchical boolean combination queries using AND, OR, or NOT.
source: Complex hierarchical boolean combination queries using AND, OR, or NOT are supported.
evidence: This describes a search capability of Taxonium.

claim: The tree in Taxonium can be panned and zoomed in the vertical and horizontal axes independently.
source: The tree, at the left hand side of the screen, can be panned, and can be zoomed in the vertical and horizontal axes independently.
evidence: This describes an interface feature demonstrated in the application.

claim: Independent zooming in vertical and horizontal axes is a crucial feature for large trees, which are invariably much larger in their y-axis.
source: The latter is a crucial feature for large trees, which are invariably much larger in their y-axis.
evidence: This is an inference about the importance of this feature based on the structure of phylogenetic trees.

claim: Taxonium provides a toggleable minimap for orientation.
source: A toggleable minimap is provided for orientation.
evidence: This describes an interface feature shown in Figure 1.

claim: Figure 1 presents a screenshot of the Taxonium web client displaying a 5,151,952 sequence tree of SARS-CoV-2 sequences.
source: This figure presents a screenshot of the Taxonium web client displaying a 5,151,952 sequence tree of SARS-CoV-2 sequences.
evidence: This is a description of Figure 1, which shows the actual interface.

claim: Taxonium supports mutation annotated trees (MATs) generated by UShER, where internal nodes are annotated with mutations inferred to have occurred at that branch of the phylogeny.
source: In addition to accepting traditional trees, Taxonium also supports mutation annotated trees (MATs, McBroome et al., 2021a), generated by UShER, where internal nodes are annotated with mutations inferred to have occurred at that branch of the phylogeny (Figure 2).
evidence: This describes a capability of Taxonium, supported by citation and demonstrated in Figure 2.

claim: An MAT essentially captures the full sequence of each sample in the tree.
source: Since an MAT essentially captures the full sequence of each sample in the tree, its use as an input permits the user to colour the tree by genotype at any desired site (Figure 3), or alternatively to search for particular mutations in internal modes (Figure 4), and to filter by how many terminal nodes these mutations gave rise to.
evidence: This is a statement about the information content of MATs, based on their design.

claim: Using an MAT as input permits the user to colour the tree by genotype at any desired site.
source: Since an MAT essentially captures the full sequence of each sample in the tree, its use as an input permits the user to colour the tree by genotype at any desired site (Figure 3), or alternatively to search for particular mutations in internal modes (Figure 4), and to filter by how many terminal nodes these mutations gave rise to.
evidence: This describes a feature enabled by MAT support, demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: MAT input allows users to search for particular mutations in internal nodes and filter by how many terminal nodes these mutations gave rise to.
source: Since an MAT essentially captures the full sequence of each sample in the tree, its use as an input permits the user to colour the tree by genotype at any desired site (Figure 3), or alternatively to search for particular mutations in internal modes (Figure 4), and to filter by how many terminal nodes these mutations gave rise to.

claim: Taxonium can allow visualisation of trees entirely in the client.
source: Taxonium can allow visualisation of trees entirely in the client (Figure 2, l.h.s.), which is especially important for trees which may contain sensitive patient-level data.
evidence: This describes a deployment mode shown in Figure 2.

claim: Client-side visualization is especially important for trees which may contain sensitive patient-level data.

claim: The Taxonium JSONL format contains a pre-computed layout for the tree, reducing the amount of computation required for its display.

claim: Newick files can be laid out in the Taxonium client using an approach heavily based on JStree.

claim: More expensive computational operations in Taxonium, such as tree sparsification, are performed in a web worker to maintain a responsive interface.

claim: The client-side only version of Taxonium permits loading trees with millions of nodes on typical consumer computers.

evidence: This is a claim about performance supported by the testing described later.

claim: The process of deserialising tree data from disk into Javascript objects in memory requires one minute and 20 seconds for a tree of 5.4 million sequences.

claim: Large trees demand increasing amounts of RAM and download bandwidth which might rule out the use of lower spec devices.

claim: In server-backed mode, a server reads trees from disk in advance and then serves required parts of them to each client on demand.
source: To allow near instantaneous access to trees with millions of nodes on almost any internet-connected device, we built a server-backed mode for Taxonium, in which a server reads trees from disk in advance and then serves required parts of them to each client on demand (Figure 2, r.h.s.).
evidence: This describes the architecture of the server-backed mode, shown in Figure 2.

claim: The server-backed mode is more efficient as it does not require all data to be sent to the client.
source: The server-backed mode is more efficient, as it does not require all data to be sent to the client, and the computationally expensive operations can be performed on a more powerful machine.
evidence: This is an inference about the efficiency benefits of the server-backed architecture.

claim: Using server-backed mode, a 5.4 million sequence tree can initially load in seconds.
source: Using this mode, a 5.4 million sequence tree can initially load in seconds.

claim: The Taxonium backend is implemented in NodeJS using Express.

claim: Memory limits in the browser can be significantly lower than the total system memory.
source: Most computers now have 8 GB or more of RAM, which is sufficient to store data from a very large tree. However memory limits in the browser can be significantly lower than the total system memory, and efficiency of storage can depend on the specific web browser, which can limit the size of trees which can be loaded locally in the Taxonium web client to ~6 M terminal nodes on some systems.

claim: Efficiency of storage in browsers can depend on the specific web browser.

evidence: This is a performance comparison result, supported by citation to the tool.

claim: Empress 1.20 did not load a 5,326,538 sequence tree in the browser in any reasonable length of time.
source: Empress 1.20 (Cantrell, 2021) did not load this tree in the browser in any reasonable length of time.

claim: Taxonium is unique among compared tools in supporting mutation-annotated trees.
source: Conversely, Taxonium is unique among these tools in supporting mutation-annotated trees, and perhaps in its ability to toggle to a time tree – features shared with, and inspired by, Auspice (Hadfield et al., 2018) – which is limited to phylogenies of <~10,000 tips (around 0.2% of Taxonium scale).
evidence: This is a comparative claim about features, supported by citation to Auspice.

claim: Taxonium is the only tool able to fluidly explore the largest trees in current use on consumer-grade hardware.
source: In sum, we argue that Taxonium is the only tool able to fluidly explore the largest trees in current use on consumer-grade hardware.

evidence: This is a speculative inference about future trends based on current observations.

claim: Taxonium is one of few tools to allow the visualisation of a mutation-annotated tree capturing all known sequence diversity in an organism.
source: Taxonium allows exploration of these large phylogenies, and is also one of few tools to allow the visualisation of a mutation-annotated tree capturing all known sequence diversity in an organism.
evidence: This is a comparative claim about Taxonium's capabilities.

claim: Some tools for phylogenetic trees are designed primarily for generating static figures suited for publications.
source: Some tools for phylogenetic trees are designed primarily for generating static figures suited for publications.

claim: Taxonium is intended primarily for exploring a tree dynamically.
source: In contrast, Taxonium is intended primarily for exploring a tree dynamically – in the case of very large trees, this is often the only way to extract useful information.
evidence: This describes the design intent of Taxonium.

claim: In the case of very large trees, dynamic exploration is often the only way to extract useful information.

claim: Artifacts in sequences are often systematic and can create entire clades brought together by shared errors.
source: Artifacts in sequences (e.g. Heguy et al., 2022; Sanderson and Barrett, 2021; Sanderson et al., 2021) are often systematic, and in such cases can create entire clades brought together by shared errors.
evidence: This is a statement about sequencing artifacts, supported by citations.

claim: In large SARS-CoV-2 phylogenies, many revertant mutations appear to represent sequencing artifacts or reversion from them.
source: In large SARS-CoV-2 phylogenies, many of these mutations appear to in fact represent sequencing artifacts, or reversion from them, and so this approach may help identify areas of a tree that have technical issues.
evidence: This is an observation from analyzing SARS-CoV-2 trees with Taxonium.

claim: Taxonium provides a search option that highlights 'revertant' mutations in which a branch apparently mutates back towards the reference genome.
source: In Taxonium, we provide a search option that highlights 'revertant' mutations in which a branch apparently mutates back towards the reference genome.
evidence: This describes a feature of Taxonium designed to identify potential artifacts.

claim: The number of tips in a particular region of the Cov2Tree tree is not always indicative of the size of an outbreak due to vastly different densities of sampling in different geographic regions.
source: A further challenge is the vastly different densities of sampling in different geographic regions. Because Cov2Tree does not downsample sequences from countries which are able to sequence a greater proportion of their cases, the number of tips in a particular region of the tree is not always indicative of the size of an outbreak, and in some cases even inferences of the directionality of migration may be confounded.
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation challenges due to sampling bias.

claim: In some cases, inferences of the directionality of migration may be confounded by different sampling densities.
source: Because Cov2Tree does not downsample sequences from countries which are able to sequence a greater proportion of their cases, the number of tips in a particular region of the tree is not always indicative of the size of an outbreak, and in some cases even inferences of the directionality of migration may be confounded.
evidence: This is an inference about potential biases in phylogeographic interpretation.
